unit.title: Earth and Beyond
unit.blurb: The Solar System and how it formed, gravity and orbits, tides, eclipses, and how our models of space developed.

O1.t: Describe the Solar System, how planets stay in orbit, days, years and seasons, and how stars and planets form from dust and gas.

O2.t: Explain tides, including spring and neap tides, using the gravity of the Moon and Sun.

O3.t: Explain solar and lunar eclipses, including umbra and penumbra.

O4.t: Describe how models of the Solar System and Universe developed as new evidence appeared.

captions: Welcome to Atomic Education.
This lesson was created by Atomic Education to help you learn Cambridge Lower Secondary Science with confidence. Let's begin!
Welcome to Unit 14: Earth and Beyond.

Have you ever looked up at the night sky and wondered how far away the stars are, or how our Solar System formed? Rockets carry satellites and probes into space to help astronomers answer these questions. Let's explore the Earth and what lies beyond it.

Our Solar System is the Sun, the planets and their moons, and everything else that orbits the Sun. The four inner planets, Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, are made mainly of rock. They're separated from the outer planets by the asteroid belt: countless pieces of rock, from pebbles to rocks many kilometres wide.
The four outer planets, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, are gas giants, made of substances like hydrogen, helium and methane. The name 'solar system' comes from 'sol', the Latin word for Sun.
Our Sun is a star: a giant sphere of very hot, glowing gas. Stars aren't star-shaped; they're round, like balls.
A planet is a large ball of rock or gas that orbits a star. Planets move around the Sun in stretched circles called elliptical orbits.
Planets don't give off their own light or heat. We see them shining because they reflect sunlight. On a clear night, you can see Venus, Mars and Jupiter without a telescope!

The Solar System is like a giant merry-go-round, with planets racing around the Sun. What holds them in place? The Sun has more than 99 percent of all the mass in the Solar System, so its gravitational force is enormous.

A planet stays in orbit because of a balance between gravity and its speed. If it moved too slowly, it would fall into the Sun. Too fast, and it would escape into space. You can model this with marbles rolling on a cloth stretched over a hoop, with a heavy ball in the middle.

All the planets except Mercury and Venus have moons. Anything that orbits a planet is a satellite: a moon is a natural satellite, and spacecraft we launch are artificial satellites. Saturn has the most known moons, and astronomers keep finding more. Its largest, Titan, is bigger than the planet Mercury!

Each planet spins on its own axis. One complete spin, or rotation, is one day on that planet. One complete orbit, or revolution, of the Sun is one year. Earth rotates once in 24 hours, and orbits the Sun in 365 and a quarter days.
Earth's axis is tilted. As we orbit the Sun, our part of the Earth points towards the Sun for part of the year, and away from it for another part. This gives us the seasons.
How do stars and planets form? It starts with a nebula: a giant cloud of gas and dust in space.

Gravity pulls the gas and dust towards the centre, and the cloud starts to spin. It speeds up and flattens into a disk. As more material falls to the centre, it gets denser and hotter, forming a ball of hot gas called a protostar.
If the temperature gets high enough, atoms fuse together into larger atoms. This is nuclear fusion, and it releases enormous amounts of energy. A star is born!

The leftover dust and gas orbiting the star cool and clump together. The clumps collide, grow, and their gravity pulls in even more material, forming planets. Rocky planets form close to the star, and gas giants further away, where it's colder. Our Solar System formed this way about 4.6 billion years ago.

stops.note: Paused after: “When the Moon is at right angles to the Sun, their pulls partly cancel out, so the differe”

q.prompt: Spring tides happen when the Sun and Moon are…

captions: At the beach, the sea level rises and falls during the day. These are tides. The Moon orbits Earth because of Earth's gravity, but the Moon's gravity also pulls on Earth, including its oceans. The ocean on the side facing the Moon bulges towards it.

There's also a bulge on the opposite side, because Earth's rotation makes the ocean fly outwards, like water swinging in a glass. As Earth turns once every 24 hours, each place passes through two bulges, giving two high tides and two low tides each day.

The Sun's gravity affects tides too, but less than the Moon's, because the Sun is so much further away. When the Sun and Moon are in line, their pulls combine, giving very high and very low tides called spring tides. They happen twice every 28 days, the time the Moon takes to orbit Earth.
When the Moon is at right angles to the Sun, their pulls partly cancel out, so the difference between high and low tide is smaller. These are neap tides.

Tides matter! Huge ships can only enter some ports at high tide, so every port has a tide table. And with sea levels rising due to climate change, people in coastal areas need to know when very high tides are coming, to protect their homes from flooding.

sections.title: Eclipses

stops.note: Paused after: “The darkest part of the shadow is the umbra; stand there, and you see a total eclipse. In ”

q.prompt: In a solar eclipse, which body is in the middle?

captions: Light travels in straight lines, so when an object blocks it, a shadow forms. A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth, casting its shadow on Earth.

The darkest part of the shadow is the umbra; stand there, and you see a total eclipse. In the lighter penumbra, you see a partial eclipse. Never look directly at the Sun, even during an eclipse: it can permanently damage your eyes! During a total eclipse, scientists can study the Sun's faint outer atmosphere, the corona.
A lunar eclipse happens when the Moon passes through Earth's shadow.
During a lunar eclipse, the Moon often looks red. Earth's atmosphere bends some sunlight onto the Moon, and removes most of the blue light, leaving red light behind.

sections.title: Developing models of space

stops.note: Paused after: “Galileo's telescopes revealed moons orbiting Jupiter and phases of Venus: evidence that no”
Paused after: “In 1846, scientists used Newton's laws to predict a new planet, Neptune, and then found it”

captions: People once believed the Earth was flat, and at the centre of the Universe. Around 100 CE, Ptolemy built a geocentric model, with Earth at the centre and everything orbiting it. He also gave us longitude and latitude.

Ancient Chinese astronomers could predict solar eclipses around 2300 BCE. Later, scientists in the Islamic world improved Ptolemy's ideas: in the 10th century, Al-Sijzi suggested that Earth rotates, and in 1261, al-Tusi listed 16 problems with Ptolemy's model.
Building on their work, Nicolaus Copernicus proposed a heliocentric model, with the Sun at the centre. Earth's spin explains why the Sun and stars appear to rise and set.

Galileo's telescopes revealed moons orbiting Jupiter and phases of Venus: evidence that not everything orbits Earth. But many people rejected the new model, choosing only the evidence that suited their opinion. That's called bias.

Our understanding kept growing. Isaac Newton's laws of gravity explained how planets stay in orbit. William Herschel built better telescopes and found Uranus, while his sister Caroline discovered comets and created a catalogue system still used today.
In 1846, scientists used Newton's laws to predict a new planet, Neptune, and then found it! Edwin Hubble showed that there are other galaxies beyond the Milky Way, and that the Universe is expanding.
Stephen Hawking showed that black holes give off radiation, and Jocelyn Bell Burnell discovered pulsars: spinning remains of stars that give off radio waves.
Old ideas are replaced or updated when new evidence comes along. That's how science works: it's an ongoing adventure of discovery!
Now it is your turn to shine! Pause the video after each question and try to answer it first.
Question 1: What keeps the planets in orbit around the Sun? Pause the video now.
Answer: The Sun's gravity, balanced by each planet's speed.
Question 2: How long does Earth take to orbit the Sun once? Pause the video now.
Answer: About 365.25 days – one year.
Question 3: When do spring tides happen? Pause the video now.
Answer: When the Sun and Moon are in line.
Question 4: What happens during a lunar eclipse? Pause the video now.
Answer: The Moon passes through Earth's shadow.
